title: 49 Transdermal effects of melatonin on horses experiencing transport stress
content:
Abstract
Transportation imposes significant physiological and psychological stress on livestock. Performance horses, in particular, often face the greatest transport stress due to their frequent participation in competitive events. The severity of this stress correlates with the duration of transport, with marked increases in heart rate, body temperature, and stress biomarkers occurring after three hours. These physiological responses are directly linked to the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the resulting release of cortisol. Melatonin, a neurotransmitter with an inverse relationship to cortisol, is known to lower heart rate and body temperature, but its effects on blood biomarkers in equine experiencing stressful conditions have not been evaluated. We hypothesized that administering a transdermal melatonin treatment could help mitigate the adverse effects of transport stress in horses. For this study, 16 horses from the Texas Tech Equestrian Center were selected for a 21-day trial. The horses were randomly allocated to one of four treatment groups in a 2x2 factorial design, with factors including the administration of melatonin (melatonin or no melatonin) and transport status (transported or not transported). The treatment groups were as follows: Control (CON) – no melatonin and no transportation; Transportation (TRS) – transported for 3 hours on day 21; Melatonin (MEL) – 24 mg/day of transdermal phytomelatonin administered over 21 days; and Melatonin plus Transportation (MELTRS) – 24 mg/day of transdermal phytomelatonin administered for 21 days, with transportation for 3 hours on day 21. On day 21 post-transport, blood was collected and evaluated for chemistry, cortisol, and melatonin. No interaction between melatonin treatment and transportation was observed for any blood variable. As expected, transported horses had higher blood cortisol levels than non-transported horses (251.20 vs. 161.3 nmoles/L; P= 0.0140). Transported horses had lower blood calcium (11.45 vs. 12.4 mmol/L; P = 0.006) and potassium (3.73 vs. 4.5; P = 0.0114) than non-transported horses, while glucose, direct bilirubin, sodium, and the sodium-to-potassium ratio were higher (P ≤ 0.0385) for transported horses. Melatonin-treated horses had significantly higher blood melatonin levels compared to untreated horses (327.25 vs. 130.8 pg/mL; P = 0.0028) and lower cortisol levels (180.25 vs. 232.21nmoles/L; P = 0.0285). Interestingly, melatonin-treated horses also exhibited higher blood urea nitrogen levels than untreated horses (17.46 vs. 15.13; P = 0.0387). In summary, transportation stress increases electrolyte precipitation and dehydration and glucose mobilization. However, transdermal melatonin may reduce cortisol levels and alleviate transport-related stress in horses, warranting further investigation into its potential benefits.
